description: Rename house.book.borrowed_by to borrowed_by_friend, and republish the view that reads it.
rationale: The column holds a friend's name, and borrowed_by read like a role or a user id. The rename itself repairs the catalog by itself: dependencies are held by OID, so house.borrowed_book stays queryable and its stored definition follows the new name with nothing rebuilt. What does NOT follow is the part people expect to -- the view keeps its OWN output column name, so its definition becomes "borrowed_by_friend AS borrowed_by" and anything reading through it still sees borrowed_by, correct and misleading, with nothing erroring to say so. Fixing that costs more than a replace: CREATE OR REPLACE VIEW can only APPEND columns, and PostgreSQL refuses outright to rename an existing one -- pg_laswell's dry run caught exactly that before anything ran. So the view is dropped and rebuilt, which is what renaming a column a view exposes actually costs. It depends on 0096 because that specification names the old column, and a rename that landed first would leave 0096 unable to parse. The explicit set_comment on the view is not redundant: replace_view emits its COMMENT ON only when it is CREATING the view, and after a drop_view in the same specification it still measures the view as present -- so the comment the drop removed is never put back. Stating it as its own intent is the reliable form.

intents.name: borrowed_book
intents.comment: Books that are out on loan, oldest loan first.
intents.definition: SELECT b.item_id, b.title, b.author, b.isbn, b.borrowed_by_friend, b.borrowed_on, CURRENT_DATE - b.borrowed_on AS days_out FROM house.book AS b WHERE b.borrowed_by_friend IS NOT NULL

intents.name: borrowed_book
intents.comment: Books that are out on loan, oldest loan first.

intents.name: borrowed_by_friend
intents.comment: Name of the friend who has the book. Null when it is home. Renamed from borrowed_by in 0099.
